content: 3. 4. Acrylamide is also known by synonyms such as propenamide, acrylic amide, and akrylamid. 5. The terms acrylamide and acrylamide monomer are used interchangeably in this document. 6. The action level for acrylamide is defined as a time-weighted average (TWA) concentration equal to half of the environmental limit. 7. It is defined as working in areas where acrylamide is stored, produced, processed, or used, except when present as an unintentional contaminant at concentrations below 1% by weight. 8. If an employee is exposed to airborne acrylamide concentrations exceeding the action level, all sections of the recommended standard must be followed. 9. 10. Procedures for collecting and analyzing environmental samples must follow the methods outlined in Appendices I and II or any equivalent method with comparable accuracy, precision, and sensitivity. 11. Medical surveillance must be provided to all individuals occupationally exposed to acrylamide. 12. Preplacement medical examinations should include comprehensive medical and work histories, with emphasis on weight loss and neurological disturbances, as well as a complete physical examination focusing on the skin, eyes, and nervous system. 13. 14. Periodic medical examinations should be conducted annually or as determined by the responsible physician. These should include interim medical and work histories, weekly examinations of exposed body areas for skin peeling, and physical examinations as outlined in the preplacement criteria. 15. 16. Medical personnel should be informed of the need for observation and follow-up for delayed neurological effects. 17. In cases of skin contact with acrylamide, contaminated clothing and shoes must be removed, and exposed areas should be thoroughly washed with soap and water. 18. If acrylamide contacts the eyes, they should be flushed with copious amounts of water, and a physician should be consulted immediately. 19. Appropriate protective clothing, such as gloves, aprons, long-sleeved overalls, footwear, and face shields, must be worn to limit skin contact with acrylamide. Impervious clothing may be required for specialized operations. 20. Eye protection, such as chemical safety goggles or face shields, must be used in operations where acrylamide may contact the eyes. 21. 22. Engineering controls should be implemented to maintain acrylamide concentrations at or below the TWA environmental limit. Respiratory protective equipment may be used during the installation or testing of these controls, emergencies, or nonroutine maintenance activities. 23. Respirators must be selected and used according to established respiratory protection programs and standards, including those approved by NIOSH and the Mining Enforcement and Safety Administration. 24. Respirators designed for higher acrylamide concentrations may be used in lower concentration environments. 25. 26. Respirators must be easily accessible, and employees must be informed of their location. 27. 28. They must also be trained in emergency procedures and safe handling practices. 29. Maintenance and repair personnel must be included in training programs, and employees must be reminded of these hazards at least annually. 30. Ventilation systems must be designed to prevent the accumulation or recirculation of acrylamide, maintain concentrations at or below the recommended limit, and effectively remove acrylamide from employees' breathing zones. 31. 32. 33. Concrete floors in operational areas must be sealed to prevent acrylamide permeation. 34. 35. Before maintenance work, sources of acrylamide and its vapor must be eliminated as much as possible. If this is not feasible, respiratory protective equipment must be used. 36. A standby worker must be present outside the confined space. 37. Emergency procedures must include prearranged plans for obtaining medical care and transporting injured workers. Employees must be trained in first aid and prepared to assist when necessary. 38. Approved eye, skin, and respiratory protection must be used during accident site cleanup. 39. 40. Eyewash fountains and showers must be provided in accordance with safety regulations. 41. 42. 43. Acrylamide is primarily manufactured from acrylonitrile through various processes, including hydration over catalysts. It is used in polymer production, soil stabilization, and water treatment. 44. 45. Workers exposed to acrylamide have reported symptoms such as numbness, tingling, weakness, and skin peeling. Neurological examinations have revealed sensory nerve damage and, in some cases, central nervous system involvement. 46. Structural nerve damage may persist in severe cases. 47.
